explain.say: Most rockets throw their boosters away, but the first stage of SpaceX's Falcon 9 flies back and lands upright so it can be used again. After separating from the upper stage, small gas thrusters flip it round.

For a landing back at the launch site, its engines fire to reverse its course. For a landing on a drone ship far out at sea, it can skip this burn and save fuel.

faq.q: How does a rocket land upright?
faq.a: It fires its engine on the way down, timed so its speed drops to almost zero just as it reaches the pad. Computers constantly adjust the engine's angle and power, and landing legs unfold at the last moment.
Grid fins are waffle-like lattice fins near the top of the booster. Folded during launch, they open on the way down and tilt to steer the falling booster through the air.
asks: What are the waffle fins on a rocket?

faq.q: How does a rocket turn around?
faq.a: Small cold-gas thrusters near the top puff nitrogen to flip the booster. Then a boostback burn of its engines sends it back towards land, if it is landing near the launch site.
Building a rocket stage costs far more than the fuel for one flight. Landing and reflying it means the expensive engines and structure are used many times, cutting the cost of reaching space.

faq.q: Why do some rockets land on ships at sea?
faq.a: Turning all the way back uses a lot of fuel. For heavy payloads, the booster instead lands on an uncrewed drone ship waiting in the ocean along its natural path.

facts: A Falcon 9 first stage first landed successfully in December 2015.
The Space Shuttle's solid rocket boosters were recovered from the ocean by parachute and reused.
